content: The test image shows corn stalks split open with internal rot — dark/black discoloration of the pith, shredded tissue, and mottled yellowish-green exterior. Key candidates: Charcoal_stalk_rot, Anthracnose_stalk_rot, Diplodia_stalk_rot.

**Analysis:**

The test image shows corn stalks split longitudinally with:
- Gray/charcoal-colored, shredded, disintegrated pith
- Tiny scattered black structures (sclerotia) throughout the pith — resembling charcoal dust or black pepper
- One stalk shows mottled yellow-green exterior with dark surface speckles
- No pink/red coloration (rules out Gibberella), no white mycelium (rules out Diplodia), no shiny black rind lesions (rules out Anthracnose)

**Comparison with references:**
- **Charcoal_stalk_rot**: The upper-left panel of the collage is nearly identical to the test image — gray shredded pith with dispersed tiny black sclerotia (Macrophomina phaseolina). This is the hallmark feature.
- **Anthracnose_stalk_rot**: Shows more brown fibrous pith and prominent shiny black external rind lesions — not matching.
- **Diplodia_stalk_rot**: Tan/brown tissue, no black sclerotia pattern.
- **Physoderma_stalk_rot**: Purple-brown at nodes, different pattern entirely.

The scattered tiny black sclerotia in gray shredded pith is the pathognomonic sign of Charcoal stalk rot.
